raw.title: Test Sieve and Give Us Feedback
raw.description:
Sieve just won our local AI browser extension bounty 🏆

Announcement here: https://x.com/i/status/2089377946066932187

Now let's see how it holds up in the real world.

## The challenge

Install Sieve, use it during your normal browsing, and put it through its paces.

GitHub here: https://github.com/Phineas1500/sieve-ai-image-detector

Try it across different websites, image types, and browsing scenarios. Look for things that work especially well, things that don't, false positives, false negatives, confusing UX, performance issues, or anything else that could make Sieve better.

Then:

1. **Post your experience publicly on X.**
2. Share what you tested and what you learned. Make sure to tag @sriramkiron, @0xSero, and @kennyistyping when you post.
3. Include specific, actionable feedback wherever possible.
4. After you post, submit a claim on this page with a screenshot of your post + its URL in the claim description.

Your feedback doesn't need to be positive. **We're looking for honest feedback that helps make Sieve better.**

## What makes a great submission?

The most valuable feedback will be specific and actionable.

For example:

* Finding a type of AI-generated image Sieve consistently misses
* Finding a type of real image it incorrectly flags
* Identifying a performance or loading issue
* Discovering a confusing part of the user experience
* Testing Sieve on an interesting real-world browsing scenario
* Suggesting a concrete improvement that makes the extension more useful

The more you can demonstrate what you found and why it matters, the better.

## The prize

This is a **winner-take-all bounty**.

The winner will be the submission that bounty contributors **find most useful and that leads to meaningful improvements to Sieve**.

This isn't a popularity contest or a writing competition. The goal is to find the feedback that actually makes the product better.

## Why we're doing this

The first bounty helped create Sieve.

This one is about putting it in the hands of real people and creating a feedback loop between users and the person building it.

If Sieve is going to become a reliable, convenient, freely available public good, it needs to be tested against the messy reality of how people actually browse the web.

So go break it. 🔍

Try Sieve, share what you find, and help make the next version better.

raw.title: 🔎 LetterLoops: The Letter Hunt
raw.description:
**How many of today's letters can you find in the real world?**

### The Challenge

Play the day's LetterLoops puzzle. 

Then find **one real-world object** containing as many of the unique letters from that day's LetterLoops answer as possible.

Take a photo of your find and submit it to the bounty.

**That's it.**

I'll verify that you completed the LetterLoops puzzle separately.

Link to LetterLoops:  https://farcaster.xyz/miniapps/x__pjJMb7ELk/letterloops

### Example

Today's LetterLoops answer is **PRACTITIONER**.

You find a **bottle of hand lotion** with physical text on the label containing **P, R, A, C, T, I, O, N, E**.

That's **9/9 unique letters** — a **Perfect Hunt. 🏆**

### The Twist

The bounty will run for several days, and **the difficulty of the Letter Hunt will change from day to day.**

Some LetterLoops answers may have common letters that are easy to find.

Others might contain uncommon letters that make the hunt much harder.

**That's part of the fun.**

You won't know what you're hunting for until you solve that day's puzzle.

You can participate on **any day during the bounty period**. You don't have to play every day.

### Rules

* You must complete the LetterLoops puzzle for the day you participate.
* Find **one real-world object** containing as many unique letters from that day's answer as possible.
* Count each unique letter only once.
* The letters must appear in **physical text** visible on the object.
* Digital screens do not count.
* The actual LetterLoops answer itself does not count.
* Don't use large blocks of text specifically because they contain lots of letters. **Dictionaries, phone books, newspapers, books, printed documents, and similar text-heavy materials don't count.**
* The object should be something you'd reasonably encounter in everyday life, not something selected primarily because it contains a large amount of text.
* The photo must be your own original photo.
* **No AI-generated images, video, or other AI-generated content.**
* Your submission should include the photo and the number of unique letters you found.

### Scoring

Your score is the number of unique letters from that day's LetterLoops answer that appear on your object.

**More letters = better score.**

If multiple submissions have the same score, the more creative or unusual find wins.

🏆 **Perfect Hunt:** Find every unique letter from that day's answer on a single object.

### The Prize

**There will be one winner.**

One participant will win **the entire prize pot**.

The puzzle might make your hunt easy.

It might make your hunt ridiculously difficult.

**You won't know until you solve it.**

Happy hunting. 🔎

Open LetterLoops:  https://farcaster.xyz/miniapps/x__pjJMb7ELk/letterloops

Vplus Laundry in Hanoi runs Ecowash machines: coin-operated washers that DualMint finances and settles the cash flow from onchain. Go stand in front of them and put it on camera.

Maps: https://maps.app.goo.gl/Xo9APa1ZDTdsr4817

What to film
  
Record yourself at the laundromat saying, on camera: "Boring works."

Then film the place. The machines mid-cycle, the space, the signage, people coming and going, whatever detail catches your eye. The point is simple. These are real washing machines, in a real laundromat, earning real money in a real city. Boring works because the machine runs the same cycle whether crypto is up or down. Most people have never seen onchain infrastructure attached to something this ordinary. That is the whole point.

After you film

Post the video to X. Tag @DualMintRWA and @poidhxyz. Add a short caption. A thought, a reaction, something about the laundromat, the machines, or the idea of owning the cash flow without owning the machine.

To claim

  - Upload a screenshot from your video as proof
  - Make sure the video clearly shows you at the laundromat
  
Bonus points for

  - Narration that tells a story
  - Capturing the atmosphere of the place
  - An interesting observation or a conversation with someone there
  - Clean editing
  - Making "machine-backed yield" feel like something you can stand next to

Housekeeping

Low-effort claims may be rejected at the reviewer's discretion. Very short clips, machines or laundromat barely visible, no commentary, or anything that doesn't actually document the location. The goal is content that genuinely shows the real-world infrastructure behind DualMint.

Respect the people there. Don't make customers or staff the focus of your video. Keep it on the machines, the space, and your own commentary. You are responsible for following local laws and the venue's rules on filming and posting.

First legit claim wins. 🏆

What is DualMint?

DualMint finances everyday machines: coin-operated laundromats, HVAC units, vending networks, arcade machines. It settles their operating revenue onchain as yield in USDC. The yield comes from quarters going into washing machines, not from token emissions or lending. A machine runs a cycle, collects the payment, and that cash flow settles onchain to depositors. Boring businesses have earned this way for decades. DualMint is how you own a piece of the cash flow without owning the machine. dualmint.com

raw.title: Help Fund A Theoretical Neuroscience Paper
raw.description:
Hi! I'm Dylan, and I've written a paper, Oscillatory Dynamics as the Coordination Layer of the Organism: Waves, Markov Blankets, and the Virtual Space of Cognition. It has been accepted by Frontiers in Neuroscience (a major journal!). All that's left is the typesetting and the open-access fee, so it can be published free for everyone, forever.
The idea came to me in a course last spring on cognitive neuroscience methods in which we studied EEG, MEG, and other brain-scanning techniques. One day we were discussing alpha waves and their inhibitory role in the brain, and I just couldn’t help thinking hey! What if the cell was actually the unit of decision making and these waves were transmitting information, instead of directly causing specific outcomes?
I took it further using a research repository I'd built, running queries against the existing literature, and landed on a synthesis I think holds up: waves carry information to cells, which then act according to need, ability, and the information contained in that signal. The paper lays out a new synthesis and ties it to a concrete, testable prediction: as the substrate degrades, aperiodic “flattening” should show up before specific oscillatory peaks disappear. If so, we may be able to leverage this behavior to detect cognitive decline much earlier in the process.
The bounty: add funds to help cover the ~$3,500 open-access publishing fee. The proof I'll submit (purely ceremonial, since this is a fundraiser) is the acceptance letter, which I already have. Contributions will be open until June 28. As a thank-you, once it's published I'll mint the final PDF of the paper on Base + Arweave and airdrop a copy to the Base Mainnet address of everyone who chipped in to help me pay for the science.
I won't pretend I've got it all figured out, but I keep a critical eye on my own ideas and I’ve tested this paper’s contents against the strongest theories and objections I could find - without breaking it. The goal is simple: get this into a serious journal, get other researchers poking at it and maybe building on it, and see if there's something here that helps people understand how bodies work. From optimizing our own cognition to prevention & treatment of disease, understanding the body is the key to the things we want to achieve. This paper is my first big effort to contribute to this project.
